passages.t: Hunted, and ‘if I have done this’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjamite” (verse 1).

The prayer starts with a run for safety: “O LORD my God, I take refuge in You; save me and deliver me from all my pursuers” (verse 1). If God does not act, they will “shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces with no one to rescue me” (verse 2).

Then the man makes a solemn statement. “O LORD my God, if I have done this, if injustice is on my hands, if I have rewarded my ally with evil, if I have plundered my foe without cause, then may my enemy pursue me and overtake me” (verses 3-5). He puts his own life on the line: if he is guilty, let the enemy trample him into the dust.
passages.hearers:
‘Shiggaion’ is a word found only here. A related form opens the prayer in Habakkuk 3:1. No one knows what it means. Some link it to a verb meaning to wander or reel, and think it names a passionate, troubled song. Others think it means a lament. It is safest to say the meaning is uncertain.

Cush the Benjamite is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. No one knows who he was. Because King Saul came from the tribe of Benjamin, many readers place the psalm in the years when Saul's men hunted David. Others think of Shimei, the Benjamite who cursed David on the road (2 Samuel 16:5-8). None of these guesses can be proved.

Whatever ‘the words of Cush’ were, they were an accusation. Someone said David had done wrong to a friend or robbed an enemy.

Verses 3 to 5 are an oath of innocence. When there were no witnesses, an accused person could swear a solemn oath before God, calling down harm on himself if he was lying. That handed the case to God. Job does the same at length in Job 31: “If I have walked in falsehood or my foot has rushed to deceit, let God weigh me with honest scales” (Job 31:5-6).

This is innocence of a specific charge. ‘If I have done this’ means this one thing I am accused of. The man is not claiming never to have sinned.

‘Selah’ follows verse 5: a musical word whose meaning is not known.
passages.later:
David's story shows such a moment. When he could have killed Saul in a cave, he cut off a corner of Saul's robe instead and said, “See and know that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands” (1 Samuel 24:11). He said, “May the LORD judge between you and me” (1 Samuel 24:12). Many readers have thought of this when reading verse 4 of the psalm, though the psalm itself does not name the moment.

Job's long oath of innocence fills Job 31.

The New Testament says that Jesus, falsely accused, “entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).
passages.asks:
Have you been accused of something you did not do? The psalm does not tell you to fight back. It tells you to take the case to God and let him judge.

It also asks for honesty. ‘If I have done this’ is a dangerous prayer. Before you pray it, look hard at your own hands.

passages.happening:
Now the man calls on God as judge. “Arise, O LORD, in Your anger; rise up against the fury of my enemies. Awake, my God, and ordain judgment” (verse 6). He pictures the nations gathered around God's throne: “take Your seat over them on high” (verse 7).

He asks for a verdict: “The LORD judges the peoples; vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity” (verse 8).

He prays for an end to evil: “Put an end to the evil of the wicked, but establish the righteous, O righteous God who searches hearts and minds” (verse 9). He rests in that: “My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart” (verse 10). “God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the picture of a law court. In Israel the judge sat while the people stood before him, and cases were often heard at the city gate. Here God takes his seat above all the nations.

‘Awake’ does not mean God was asleep. It is a bold way of saying: act now, do not wait.

‘Vindicate me’ means: show that I am in the right. ‘According to my righteousness and integrity’ again means in this case. He is asking God to judge the charge against him, not his whole life.

‘Hearts and minds’ in verse 9 is, in Hebrew, ‘hearts and kidneys’. In Hebrew thought the kidneys stood for a person's deepest feelings and motives, much as English speaks of the gut. God sees not only what people did, but why.

‘Indignation’ in verse 11 means anger at wrong. A judge who did not care about injustice would be no judge at all. God feels it ‘each day’.
passages.later:
Jeremiah prays in almost the same words: “O LORD of Hosts, who judges righteously, who examines the heart and mind” (Jeremiah 11:20). God says, “I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10).

The risen Jesus says the same of himself in Revelation: “I am the One who searches minds and hearts” (Revelation 2:23).
passages.hard:
‘According to my righteousness and integrity.’ Is this pride? Is the man claiming to be perfect?

No. He has just named the charge against him: ‘if I have done this’. He asks God to judge that charge. He is innocent of what he is accused of. That is all.

The same book is full of confession. Psalm 51 begs, ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’ Psalm 130 asks who could stand if God kept a record of sins. The psalmists knew they were sinners. They also knew the difference between being a sinner and being guilty of a lie someone told about you.

The book page on the Psalms says more about these claims of innocence. Christians also read such prayers as prayers that one person, Jesus, could pray in full truth, and that others pray as people made right with God through him.
passages.asks:
God searches hearts and kidneys, the hidden reasons as well as the deeds. Ask what he finds in yours, under what others see.

That can be frightening. It can also be a relief: when you are misjudged, there is one judge who sees all of it.

passages.t: The pit he dug, and a song of thanks
passages.happening:
The psalm warns the wicked: “If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword; He has bent and strung His bow” (verse 12). “He has prepared His deadly weapons; He ordains His arrows with fire” (verse 13).

Then it shows how evil grows: “Behold, the wicked man travails with evil; he conceives trouble and births falsehood” (verse 14). And how it ends: “He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making” (verse 15). “His trouble recoils on himself, and his violence falls on his own head” (verse 16).

The man ends with thanks: “I will thank the LORD for His righteousness and sing praise to the name of the LORD Most High” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Verse 12 begins with ‘If one does not repent’. Even here, there is a door left open. The weapons are ready, but the call to turn comes first.

God as a warrior with sword and bow was a picture any ancient reader knew from kings and their armies. Here the warrior is the judge of all the earth.

Verse 14 uses the picture of a pregnancy in three stages. ‘Travails’ means labours, as in giving birth. Evil is conceived as an idea, grows inside, and is born as a lie. The poem shows how wrongdoing starts within and comes out into the world.

The pit is a hunter's trap: a hole dug and covered, so that an animal falls in. The man who dug it falls in himself. In many psalms God's judgment works this way: evil turns back on the one who does it.

‘LORD Most High’ is a title for God as ruler over all. Psalm 9 takes it up at once (9:2).
passages.later:
Proverbs says the same: “He who digs a pit will fall into it” (Proverbs 26:27). Paul writes, “Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return” (Galatians 6:7).

James uses the same picture of evil being born: “after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (James 1:15).
passages.asks:
Verse 14 asks you to notice where wrong begins: as a thought, before it is a deed. Ask what you are carrying that could grow into harm, and bring it to God while it is still small.

And the end of the psalm asks something else: to thank God for his justice, even before you see it done.
